edge.title: The gold with a story attached
edge.setup: A stranger or a friend-of-a-friend has gold — inherited, found, blessed, or 'from a closed jeweller'. He will sell it well below market, or hand you a little as proof and offer more if you put money in. The story is detailed and slightly sacred, and there is a reason it must stay quiet.
edge.tell: A price below market, with a story that explains why it must be quick and secret.
move: Never pay, lend or hand over anything before the metal is tested. A small sample being real is the bait, not the proof.
Test at a BIS-hallmarked jeweller or an assay centre of your choosing, not one the seller suggests.
Buy gold only from a registered jeweller who gives a bill and hallmarked pieces. If a seller refuses a bill, that refusal is the answer.
If you have already paid, report on 1930 or cybercrime.gov.in, and to the local police, the same day.
edge.why: A genuine bargain does not need a secret, a sacred reason or a deadline. The story exists to make you skip the one step that kills the con, which is verification. The secrecy also stops you from asking someone who would say no.
edge.variants: Same shape: 'treasure' found while digging, double-your-money schemes, a tout selling 'seized' goods cheap, crypto 'insider tips'.

lens.name: Principal–agent problem
lens.one_line: The person acting for you is paid for something subtly different from what you want.
lens.detail: A broker is paid when a deal closes, not when you choose well. An insurance agent is paid on commission, which differs by product. A contractor is paid for the job, not for the job lasting. None of this requires bad intent — the incentive is enough. Knowing the pay structure predicts the advice better than knowing the person.
elsewhere: Fund managers judged quarterly take risks that look fine quarterly.
A politician's horizon is the next election; infrastructure's horizon is thirty years.
A mechanic paid per part replaced finds more parts to replace.
lens.test: Before weighing advice, ask: what exactly triggers this person getting paid?
lens.today: Farmers poured hundreds of litres of milk at a society in Bengaluru after getting no Dasara bonus (Times of India). The society sits between farmers and the buyer, so the useful question is not who is right but what each side is paid for and when. The same question works on any broker, agent or intermediary you deal with this week.

moved.what: Liquor sales curbs apply from 21 October for Dasara processions and MLC polls (Times of India).
moved.so_what: Expect procession diversions and slow roads today; buy anything you need now, and leave early in the rain.

moved.what: Farmer groups have called a statewide protest on 23 October (Times of India).
moved.so_what: Check the route before travelling that day, especially intercity, and keep a buffer for delays.

moved.what: Tomato prices have crashed by up to 80% in Bengaluru, but the drop is not city-wide (Times of India).
moved.so_what: Check your own market's rate before stocking up; 80% is the best case, not your vendor's price.

moved.what: The Bengaluru-Mumbai Vande Bharat sleeper is likely to run its inaugural trip on 1 November, a 16-hour journey (Times of India, Deccan Herald).
moved.so_what: If you need Mumbai around that week, watch IRCTC for fares and booking windows before they fill.

moved.what: About 1.3 lakh consumers have refused to share documents and opted out of the Jyothi power scheme (Times of India).
moved.so_what: If you are asked for documents under the scheme, find out what you would lose by opting out before you ignore the request.

moved.what: Jio's IPO has opened for public bids in a record $3.2 billion sale (Reuters).
moved.so_what: If you apply, do it only through your own broker or UPI app; anyone offering guaranteed allotment or a tip by message is the scam.

carry_over.prompt: A call says a courier in your name is held and a small fee will release it: what is the tell?
carry_over.answer: An unexpected problem whose solution is a small immediate payment to a stranger.
